opus-5.5.text:
I think it's essential, honestly, because without clinicians you can very easily build something that's technically impressive but clinically useless. As computer scientists and data scientists, we're good at building models and optimizing metrics, but we don't always know which questions actually matter at the bedside, or what a meaningful outcome looks like for a patient.

Clinicians bring that context. They know where the real pain points are in a workflow, what decisions they're struggling with, and what information would change how they treat someone. They also understand the data in a way we often don't. Medical data is messy. There are reasons a test was ordered, or not ordered, and reasons certain images look the way they do, and if you don't understand that, your model can learn shortcuts that have nothing to do with the underlying biology.

Then there's adoption. If clinicians haven't been part of the process from the beginning, they're far less likely to trust the tool or use it. Bringing them in early, having them help define the problem, interpret results, and challenge our assumptions, makes the work better and much more likely to reach patients.

So for me it's a true partnership. The best projects I've been part of started with a clinician coming to us with a problem they cared deeply about, and then we worked through it together. That's where the real impact comes from.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers can build something technically impressive but clinically useless, which clearly conveys that an impressive medical AI idea can lack clinical value.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention publicly releasing medical datasets or research groups competing to answer a shared question.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think it's the whole ballgame. I came into this field as a computer scientist, and very early on I learned that if you build something in isolation, you end up solving a problem nobody actually has. You can get a beautiful model with great accuracy on a benchmark, and it turns out the question it answers isn't the question a surgeon is asking at seven in the morning before they go into the operating room.

So for me, collaboration with clinicians does a few things. First, it shapes the question. A radiologist or an oncologist knows where the real uncertainty is in their day. They know which decisions keep them up at night, and those are the places where a tool can actually change outcomes. That's very different from picking a problem because a dataset happens to be available.

Second, it keeps you honest about the data. Medical data is messy. Scans come from different machines, labels are made by people with different levels of experience, and the thing you're predicting might have been recorded inconsistently for twenty years. A clinician will look at your training set and say, "Oh, that cohort is all from the one hospital that uses a different contrast protocol." You would never catch that on your own, and it's exactly the kind of thing that makes a model fall apart when it meets the real world.

And third, there's the question of trust and adoption. If a model is going to sit in a clinical workflow, the people using it need to understand what it's doing and when to be skeptical of it. That only happens if they were in the room while it was built. I've spent a lot of my career working alongside surgeons at the bench, so to speak, and the projects that went somewhere were always the ones where the clinician was a true partner, not just someone who handed over data and waited for a paper.

So I'd say it's not a nice-to-have. If the goal is to actually help patients, you can't do medical AI without clinicians. You can do machine learning on medical data, but that's a different thing.

r001.rationale: The response says an accurate, impressive model built in isolation may answer a question clinicians do not actually need solved, so it can lack clinical value.

r002.rationale: The response discusses messy medical data and clinician collaboration, but does not describe publicly releasing datasets so research groups can compete to answer a shared question.

As AI researchers, we can build something technically impressive, but if it doesn’t address a real clinical need or fit into how care is delivered, it may never be useful. Working with clinicians helps us ask the right questions, understand what the data can and can’t tell us, and evaluate whether a model could make a meaningful difference. That collaboration needs to happen from the beginning, so we’re developing something together that can ultimately improve patient care.

sol-6.1.text: Collaboration with clinicians is essential because they understand the problems that matter in patient care. As AI researchers, we can develop sophisticated methods, but we need clinical expertise to understand what the data represents, where it may be misleading, and whether our results would actually help someone make a decision. That collaboration should start with defining the question and continue through evaluating the work. Ultimately, the goal is to improve care, and that requires building something that fits the clinical setting.
